items: Baseline investigations
Clinical assessment and TB symptom review
Sputum Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra or another WHO-recommended rapid molecular test
Sputum smear microscopy for acid-fast bacilli, where indicated
Mycobacterial culture and drug-susceptibility testing, as indicated
Chest X-ray for pulmonary TB assessment
HIV test and counselling
FBC
Liver function tests: ALT, AST, bilirubin
Renal function: urea, creatinine, eGFR
Baseline visual acuity and colour vision before ethambutol when feasible
Pregnancy test where relevant
Hepatitis B/C testing where risk factors or clinical indications exist

blocks.text: Blood glucose or HbA1c, particularly in patients at risk of diabetes

items: Additional investigations according to presentation
Lymph node aspirate/biopsy for suspected extrapulmonary TB
CSF studies and neuroimaging for suspected TB meningitis
Pleural fluid studies for suspected pleural TB
Abdominal ultrasound or CT for suspected abdominal TB
ECG when QT-prolonging drugs or cardiac risk factors are relevant
Hearing assessment when injectable aminoglycosides are used
Drug-resistance testing when rifampicin resistance or treatment failure is suspected
Before and during treatment
Review drug interactions, especially with antiretroviral therapy
Review alcohol use and hepatotoxicity risk
Assess previous TB treatment and drug resistance risk
Educate on adherence and adverse effects
Monitor symptoms, sputum conversion and treatment response

blocks.text: Repeat liver or renal tests when indicated by symptoms, risk factors or regimen

subsections.subsection_title: HIV Antiretroviral Therapy: First, Second and Third Line

rows: TDF: renal toxicity, reduced bone mineral density; 3TC: headache, rare pancreatitis; DTG: insomnia, headache, weight gain
TAF + 3TC + DTG; ABC + 3TC + DTG in selected patients
TAF: weight gain, lipid changes; ABC: hypersensitivity reaction, HLA-B*57:01 association
Optimised NRTI backbone + boosted darunavir (DRV/r or DRV/c), or an appropriate boosted PI-based regimen; DTG-based options depend on prior regimen and resistance
Darunavir: GI upset, rash, hepatotoxicity; ritonavir/cobicistat: drug interactions, dyslipidaemia
Resistance-guided combinations: DRV/r, DTG, and/or other fully active agents such as fostemsavir, ibalizumab, maraviroc or enfuvirtide, depending on resistance and availability
Enfuvirtide: injection-site reactions; maraviroc: hepatotoxicity, postural hypotension; fostemsavir: nausea, QT prolongation risk; ibalizumab: diarrhoea, rash

blocks.text: Common ART adverse effects: nausea, diarrhoea, headache, rash, sleep disturbances, metabolic abnormalities.
Efavirenz: vivid dreams, dizziness, neuropsychiatric effects.
Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate: proximal renal tubulopathy, Fanconi syndrome, osteomalacia.
Protease inhibitors: dyslipidaemia, insulin resistance, drug interactions.
Nevirapine, efavirenz and zidovudine: older regimens; use depends on current national guidelines and clinical circumstances.

subsections.subsection_title: Aspirin — Conditions in Which It Is Used

items: Antiplatelet indications
Acute coronary syndrome (ACS)
Acute myocardial infarction
Secondary prevention after myocardial infarction
Secondary prevention after non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke or TIA
Established coronary artery disease

blocks.text: After selected coronary interventions/stenting, usually as part of a defined antiplatelet regimen

items: Symptomatic peripheral arterial disease
Selected patients after coronary artery bypass grafting
Other indications
Kawasaki disease
Selected pregnancy patients for pre-eclampsia prevention, under obstetric guidance
Not routinely indicated
Primary prevention in most adults without established cardiovascular disease
Atrial fibrillation as a substitute for anticoagulation
Haemorrhagic stroke
Active significant bleeding
Aspirin allergy or aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease
Cautions
Peptic ulcer disease or GI bleeding
Thrombocytopenia
Bleeding disorders
Severe renal impairment
Children with viral illnesses (Reye syndrome risk)
Acute symptomatic hypocalcaemia
Hypocalcaemic tetany
Hypocalcaemic seizures
Calcium replacement in selected cases of severe hypocalcaemia
Cardiac membrane stabilisation in severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes
Calcium-channel blocker toxicity, as an adjunct
Hypermagnesaemia with cardiac or neuromuscular toxicity

blocks.text: Hydrofluoric acid exposure — systemic calcium replacement and selected local treatments under specialist protocols

items: Calcium replacement during massive transfusion when clinically indicated
Important precautions
Does not lower serum potassium in hyperkalaemia
ECG monitoring for IV administration in emergencies
Avoid extravasation; tissue injury may occur
Use caution in patients taking digoxin
Do not mix with bicarbonate- or phosphate-containing solutions

blocks.text: In neonates, avoid simultaneous administration with ceftriaxone due to precipitation risk

items: High-yield cautions

Ipratropium: dry mouth; avoid eye exposure, especially in narrow-angle glaucoma

Budesonide: oral candidiasis; rinse mouth after use
